en: Dīgha Nikāya 29,
The Pāsādika Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a palace in the mango grove of the Sakyans named Vedhaññā.
Now at that time, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta had recently passed away at Pāvā.
Following his death, the Nigaṇṭhas were split and divided, having fallen into disputes, quarrels, and contention; they lived attacking one another with verbal weapons, saying:
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline.
How could you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly. My [practice] is consistent; yours is inconsistent.
What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first. You have overstepped [the bounds].”
"You have been turned back; your argument has been refuted; you are defeated. Go forth to seek deliverance from your position, or provide an explanation if you are able.
Indeed, it seems as though there is nothing but slaughter among the Nigaṇṭhas, followers of Nātaputta.
Even those who are the lay disciples of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, dressed in white, [behave thus] among the Nigaṇṭhas, followers of Nātaputta.

They were disillusioned with form, detached from form, and turned away from form— just as one would be toward a poorly proclaimed and poorly expounded Dhamma and Vinaya that is not conducive to liberation,
not conducive to peace, not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One, whose monuments have crumbled, and which offers no refuge. Then the novice Cunda,
having completed the rains retreat at Pāvā, approached the village of Sāma where the Venerable Ānanda was staying.
Having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the novice Cunda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta has recently passed away in Pāvā."
“With his passing away, the Nigaṇṭhas have split and become divided... [as before] ...with their monuments broken and without a refuge.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the novice Cunda:
“Friend Cunda, this is a subject that merits bringing it before the Blessed One for an audience.”
"Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we shall report this matter to the Blessed One.
"Very well, venerable sir," the novice Cunda replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda went to where the Blessed One was; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this novice monk Cunda says: 'Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta has recently passed away at Pāvā.'"
“With his passing away, the Nigaṇṭhas will split apart...
[as before] ...with their monuments shattered and left without a refuge.

“It is indeed so, Cunda, that in a Dhamma and Vinaya that is poorly proclaimed, poorly expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One, this happens.”

In this case, Cunda, there is a teacher who is not a perfectly enlightened Buddha; and the Dhamma is ill-proclaimed, ill-expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not proclaimed by a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
and a disciple dwells in that Dhamma without practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, without practicing correctly, and without living according to the Dhamma, and he turns away from that Dhamma.
He should be addressed thus:

"Friend, it is a gain for you, it is well-acquired by you, that your teacher is not a perfectly enlightened Buddha, and that the Dhamma is ill-proclaimed, ill-expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not proclaimed by a perfectly enlightened Buddha.

And you, in regard to that Dhamma, do not dwell practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, nor practicing with proper conduct, nor living in conformity with the Dhamma; rather, having departed from that Dhamma, you act according to your own whims."
Thus, Cunda, in such a case the Teacher is to be censured, the Dhamma is to be censured, and the disciple is to be praised in this way.
Cunda, if anyone were to say of such a disciple:
"Let this venerable one practice exactly as the Dhamma has been taught and laid down by his Teacher," [he would be speaking rightly].
He who incites, he whom he incites, and he who, being incited, practices accordingly—all these produce much demerit.
Why is that? Because, Cunda, it is so with a poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, badly expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.

But here, Cunda, there is a teacher who is not a perfectly enlightened Buddha; and the Dhamma is ill-proclaimed, ill-expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and proclaimed by one who is not a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Yet a disciple dwells practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing correctly, living in accordance with the Dhamma, and conducts himself having undertaken that Dhamma.
He should be addressed thus:

‘Friend, it is a loss for you, it is poorly gained by you; your Teacher is not a Fully Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is ill-proclaimed, ill-expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not proclaimed by a Fully Enlightened One.
And you dwell in that Dhamma practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing correctly, living according to the Dhamma, having undertaken that Dhamma, you conduct yourself accordingly.
In this way, Cunda, the Teacher there is to be censured, the Dhamma there is to be censured, and the disciple there is likewise to be censured.
Cunda, whoever would say of such a disciple as this:

"Surely this venerable one has entered upon the right way and will attain the goal," and whoever praises him—both the one who praises and the one who is praised—exert even greater energy; all of them generate much demerit.

And why is that? Because it is so, Cunda, with regard to a Dhamma and Vinaya that is poorly proclaimed, poorly expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.
2. The Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.

But here, Cunda, there is a teacher who is a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha), and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the perfectly enlightened Buddha;

yet a disciple does not dwell practicing in accordance with that Dhamma, nor does he practice properly, nor does he live according to the Dhamma, but having departed from that Dhamma, he acts contrary to it.
He should be addressed thus:
"Friend, it is a loss for you, it is ill-gotten for you, that while the Teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, well-expounded, leading out, conducive to peace,
and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One, you do not dwell practicing in accordance with that Dhamma, you do not practice with proper conduct, you do not live according to the Dhamma,
and having departed from that Dhamma, you act otherwise. Thus, Cunda, in that case the Teacher is to be praised, the Dhamma is to be praised, and the disciple is to be thus censured.
Cunda, if someone were to say of such a disciple:
“Let this venerable one practice in such a way as the Dhamma has been taught and laid down by his Teacher,” then the one who encourages him,
the one who is encouraged, and the one who, being encouraged, practices accordingly— all of them produce much merit.
For what reason?
Because, Cunda, it is thus with a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya that is well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.

Moreover, Cunda, here there is a Teacher who is a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.

And if a disciple dwells practicing in accordance with that Dhamma, practicing correctly, living in conformity with the Dhamma, and conducts himself having undertaken that Dhamma, he should be addressed thus:
"It is a gain for you, friend; it is well-gained by you."
"The Teacher is a Fully Enlightened One for you; the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One.
And you dwell practicing that Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing with propriety, living according to the Dhamma, having undertaken that Dhamma, and conducting yourself accordingly.
Thus, Cunda, in this case the Teacher is praiseworthy, the Dhamma is praiseworthy, and the disciple is likewise praiseworthy.
Cunda, whoever might say of such a disciple as this:
“Surely this venerable one has entered upon the right way and will attain the goal,” both he who speaks thus and he whom he praises—
indeed, whoever praises him and whoever, being praised, exerts even greater energy— all of them generate much merit.
And why is that? Because it is so, Cunda, in a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
3. The Teacher Who Does Not Grieve for His Disciples.

But here, Cunda, a Teacher has arisen in the world who is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One;

yet his disciples are not proficient in the True Dhamma, and the holy life in its entirety, in its full perfection, has not been revealed, made plain, formulated in all its details, established with its wonders, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
Then their Teacher passes away.
Such a Teacher, Cunda, is regretted by his disciples after he has passed away.
And for what reason?

‘The Teacher has arisen in the world for us—an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and made known by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Yet we are unskilled in the meaning of the True Dhamma, and the holy life in its entirety, in its full perfection, has not been revealed and laid bare for us with all its constituent parts.’
"It was accompanied by wonders and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
Now our Teacher has passed away.
Cunda, such a teacher as this is regretted by his disciples after he has died.

4. A Teacher Whose Disciples Have No Cause for Remorse Furthermore, Cunda, a Teacher has arisen in the world who is an arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha). The Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out [from suffering], conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
And his disciples have realized the meaning of the true Dhamma; they have fulfilled the entire holy life (brahmacariya) in its completeness.
It has been revealed, laid bare, made into a comprehensive summary, established with its demonstration, and well-proclaimed as far as gods and humans.
Then the Teacher passes away.
Such, Cunda, is a teacher who, having passed away, is not to be regretted by his disciples.
And why is that? “Our Teacher has arisen in the world, an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha.
And the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened One.”

“We have been instructed in the true Dhamma, and the holy life has been revealed to us in its entirety, made fully complete, laid bare, formulated with all its constituent parts, and established with its wonders, well-proclaimed as far as gods and humans.
Then our Teacher passes away. Such, Cunda, is a teacher who, having passed away, is not to be grieved for by his disciples.
5. Discourse on the Non-Fulfillment of the Holy Life “Cunda,
even if the holy life is endowed with these factors, if there is no teacher who is an elder, of long standing, long-ordained, advanced in years,
and reached the final stage of life, then that holy life is incomplete in that respect.”
But when, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these factors, and there is a teacher who is an elder, of long standing, long-ordained, advanced in years,
and come to the last stage of life— then that holy life is complete in that respect.
And even if, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these factors, and there is a teacher who is an elder, of long standing...

He has long been gone forth, advanced in years, and reached the end of his life; yet he does not have elder bhikkhus as his disciples who are experienced, disciplined, confident, and have attained security from bondage.
He is not capable of fully proclaiming the true Dhamma, nor of refuting the doctrines of others that have arisen with reasoned arguments and teaching the Dhamma accompanied by miracles.
In this way, that holy life is incomplete in that respect.
But when, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these very factors, and there is a teacher who is an elder,
of long standing, long ordained, advanced in years, and come to the last stage of life, and his bhikkhu disciples are elders— then it is complete.
They become competent, disciplined, confident, and have attained security from bondage.
They are capable of proclaiming the true Dhamma; they are capable of refuting, with reasoned arguments, the doctrines of others that have arisen, and of teaching the Dhamma with its wonders.
In this way, that holy life becomes complete in that respect.
Cunda, even if the holy life is endowed with these factors, and there is a teacher who is an elder,
of long standing, long ordained, advanced in years, and come to the final stage of life; and if there are elder bhikkhu disciples who are proficient,
disciplined, confident, and have attained security from bondage.
He is capable of proclaiming the true Dhamma; he is capable of refuting, with reasoned arguments, the doctrines of others that have arisen, and of teaching the Dhamma with its wonders.
Yet he has no middle-ranking bhikkhu disciples...
[and so on] ...he has middle-ranking bhikkhu disciples, but he has no junior bhikkhu disciples... [and so on].
He has junior bhikkhus as disciples, but he does not have elder bhikkhunīs as female disciples … [and so on] … he has elder bhikkhunīs as female disciples,

but he does not have middle-ranking bhikkhunīs as female disciples … [and so on] … he has middle-ranking bhikkhunīs as female disciples, but he does not have junior bhikkhunīs as female disciples … [and so on].
He has female bhikkhunīs as his disciples, but he does not have male lay followers who are white-robed celibates; ... [and so on] ...
he has male lay followers who are white-robed celibates, but he does not have male lay followers who are white-robed enjoyers of sensual pleasures; ... [and so on] ...
he has male lay followers who are white-robed enjoyers of sensual pleasures, but he does not have female lay followers who are white-robed celibates; ... [and so on] ...

He has female lay disciples who are householders dressed in white and living the celibate life; yet he does not have female lay disciples who are householders dressed in white and enjoying sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he has female lay disciples who are householders dressed in white and enjoying sensual pleasures;
yet his holy life is not successful, prosperous, widespread, well-known, and far-famed, reaching as far as the world of gods and humans, and well-proclaimed... [as before] ...

And his holy life is successful, prosperous, widespread, well-known to many, far-reaching, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans, yet it has not reached the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame.
In this way, that holy life is incomplete in that respect.
But when, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these very factors and the Teacher—
There is an elder who is long-standing, long-ordained, advanced in years, and has reached the final stage of life;
he has senior monks as his disciples who are competent, disciplined, confident, and have attained security from bondage.
He is capable of proclaiming the true Dhamma, and capable of refuting the doctrines of others that have arisen by means of reasoned arguments, and of teaching the Dhamma with its wonders.
His middle-ranking bhikkhu disciples are present;
his newly ordained bhikkhu disciples are present;
and his elder bhikkhunī disciples are present.
He has middle-ranking bhikkhunīs as his female disciples;
he has newly ordained bhikkhunīs as his female disciples;
he has lay male disciples; and there are white-robed householders who lead the holy life.
His male lay disciples (upāsakas) are householders dressed in white who enjoy sensual pleasures;
his female lay disciples (upāsikās) are householders dressed in white who lead the holy life (brahmacārinī);
and his female lay disciples are householders dressed in white who enjoy sensual pleasures.
And his holy life is successful, flourishing, widespread, well-known by many, far-reaching, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans; it has attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame.
In this way, that holy life is complete in that respect.
But as for me, Cunda, I have now appeared in the world as a teacher, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha.
The Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

My disciples have understood the meaning of the True Dhamma; and the entire holy life has been revealed, laid bare, made complete in all its aspects, established with its wonders, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
But now, Cunda, I am the Teacher who is aged, long-veteran, long-ordained, advanced in years, and has reached the final stage of life.
Furthermore, Cunda, there are now elder bhikkhus who are my disciples—competent, disciplined, confident, and attained to security from bondage;

they are capable of proclaiming the true Dhamma, and capable of refuting, with reasons consistent with the Dhamma, the doctrines of others that have arisen, and of teaching the Dhamma accompanied by miracles.
Furthermore, Cunda, there are now middle-ranking bhikkhus who are my disciples…
Furthermore, Cunda, I now have junior bhikkhu disciples...
Furthermore, Cunda, I now have elder bhikkhunī disciples...
Furthermore, Cunda, I now have middle-aged bhikkhunī disciples...
Furthermore, Cunda, I now have nine bhikkhunī disciples...
Furthermore, Cunda, I now have lay male disciples who are white-robed householders practicing the holy life...
Furthermore, Cunda, I now have lay male disciples who are white-robed householders enjoying sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, Cunda, I now have female lay disciples who are white-robed householders living the holy life;
furthermore, Cunda, I now have female lay disciples who are white-robed householders enjoying sensual pleasures.
Now, Cunda, my holy life is successful, flourishing, widespread, well-known to many, and far-reaching, well-proclaimed among both gods and humans.
"Cunda, as far as the teachers who have arisen in the world at present, I do not see even a single other teacher who has attained such excellence in gain and excellence in fame as I have.
And Cunda, as far as the Saṅghas or groups that have arisen in the world at present,
I do not see even a single other Saṅgha that has attained such excellence in gain and excellence in fame as this Bhikkhu Saṅgha, Cunda."
Cunda, one who would speak rightly of that which is "the holy life well-proclaimed,
complete in all its aspects, fulfilled in all its aspects, without deficiency or excess, absolute,
and perfectly manifested," would be speaking rightly of this very thing.
‘Endowed with all aspects... well-expounded.
Cunda, Udaka Rāmaputta indeed speaks these words:
‘One who sees does not see.’
And what is it that one does not see while seeing?
One sees the surface of a well-sharpened razor, but one does not see its edge.
This is called:
‘Seeing, one does not see.
Now, Cunda, what was spoken by Uddaka Rāmaputta—that which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—was said with reference only to a razor.
And as for that which one might rightly say:
‘Seeing, one does not see’—this is what one would rightly say when saying:
‘Seeing, one does not see.
And what is it that, while seeing, one does not see?
Thus he sees: "The holy life has been well-proclaimed—endowed with all aspects, fulfilled in all aspects, neither deficient nor redundant, absolute, complete, and perfectly articulated.
He does not see anything here that he could remove, thinking, "By thus removing it, this would become even more pure.
He does not see anything here that he could add, thinking, "By thus adding it, this would become more complete."
This, Cunda, is called ‘seeing,
one does not see. And as to that,
Cunda, one who speaks rightly might say:

‘The holy life has been perfectly proclaimed in all its aspects…’— speaking rightly, one would say this very thing: [that the Blessed One is the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One].”
‘The holy life has been well-proclaimed by me—complete in all its aspects, fulfilled in all its aspects, neither deficient nor superfluous, perfect and pure.
6. The Teachings to be Chanted Together:
Therefore, Cunda, as for those teachings that have been taught to you by me through direct knowledge, you should all come together and assemble there.
The meaning should be recited together with the meaning, and the phrasing with the phrasing;

one must not dispute them, so that this holy life may endure for a long time and remain stable. That would be for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
And what, Cunda, are those teachings taught by me through direct knowledge, wherein all of you, having come together and assembled,
should recite the meaning with the meaning and the phrasing with the phrasing, without disputing,
so that this holy life may endure for a long time and remain stable, for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world?
For the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans?

That is to say: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
These, Cunda, are the teachings taught by me through direct knowledge.
Wherever all of you, having come together and assembled, should recite word for word and meaning for meaning, without disputing,
so that this holy life may endure and remain long-lasting—
for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
7. The Procedure for Admonishing.

Furthermore, Cunda, while you are training together in concord, with mutual joy and without dispute, if some fellow in the holy life should speak on the Dhamma within the Saṅgha, and it should occur to you:
‘This venerable one indeed grasps the meaning wrongly and construes the phrasing wrongly.
One should neither rejoice in this nor reject it; without rejoicing and without rejecting, one should say to him:
‘Friend, between these phrasings for this meaning—these or those—which are more appropriate? And between this meaning and that meaning for these phrasings—which is more appropriate?’”
If he should say:
"Friend, these very words for this meaning are more appropriate than those; and this very meaning for these words is more appropriate than that," one should neither praise him nor disparage him.
Without praising or disparaging, one should carefully convince him to attend to both that meaning and those words.
Furthermore, Cunda, if another fellow practitioner of the holy life should speak the Dhamma in the Saṅgha,
and if you should think of him:
‘This venerable one indeed grasps the meaning wrongly but sets forth the phrasing correctly.’
Neither should one rejoice in it nor reject it; without rejoicing and without rejecting, one should say this to him:
"Friend, regarding these words, is this the meaning or that the meaning—which is more appropriate?
If he should say this:
"Friends, among these expressions, this very meaning is indeed more appropriate, namely that which [I have stated].
He should neither be praised nor disparaged; without praising or disparaging, he should be thoroughly persuaded toward a careful consideration of that very meaning.
Furthermore, Cunda, if another fellow practitioner of the holy life should speak the Dhamma in the Saṅgha...
In that case, if you should think:
"This venerable one indeed grasps the meaning correctly but misplaces the phrasing," you should neither rejoice in it nor reject it.
Without rejoicing and without rejecting, he should be addressed thus:
‘Friend, regarding this meaning, which of these two sets of phrasing—these or those—is more appropriate?
If he should say:
‘Friend, regarding this meaning, these very phrases are more appropriate than those.’”
Therefore, he should neither be praised nor disparaged; without praising or disparaging, he should instead thoroughly convince him by means of those very same words.
Furthermore, Cunda, if another fellow practitioner of the holy life should speak the Dhamma in the Saṅgha, and you should think thus:
‘This venerable one indeed grasps both the meaning correctly and sets forth the phrasing correctly.
His statement ‘Excellent! should be welcomed and rejoiced in;
having welcomed and rejoiced in his statement ‘Excellent!’, he should be addressed as follows:

“It is a gain for us, friends! It is a great fortune for us, friends, that we see such a venerable companion in the holy life, so endowed with both meaning and phrasing. 8. The Reason for Allowing Requisites The Blessed One said: “Monks, I allow you these four requisites: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for use in sickness. Monks thought: “How many kinds of robes does the Blessed One allow? They asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many kinds of robes does the Blessed One allow? “Monks, I allow three kinds of robes: the hempen robe, the jute robe, and the cotton robe. I allow these three kinds of robes. “Venerable sir, how many kinds of almsbowls does the Blessed One allow? “I allow two kinds of almsbowls: the iron bowl and the clay bowl. I allow these two kinds of almsbowls. “Venerable sir, how many kinds of lodgings does the Blessed One allow?

“I allow five kinds of lodgings: a dwelling, a gabled house, a cell, a mansion, and a cave. I allow these five kinds of lodgings. “Venerable sir, how many kinds of medicinal requisites for use in sickness does the Blessed One allow? “I allow four kinds of medicinal requisites for use in sickness: ghee, fresh butter, oil, and honey. These may be kept for seven days and then consumed; beyond that, they are not to be consumed. I allow these four kinds of medicinal requisites for use in sickness. Thus was the reason for allowing the requisites taught. Thus was the first section on the allowance of requisites concluded. This is called the *Paccayānuññātakāraṇa*. Thus was the eighth chapter, the *Paccayānuññātakāraṇa*, concluded. This is called the *Mahāvagga*. Thus was the first section of the *Mahāvagga* concluded. This is called the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkhuddesa*. Thus was the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha* concluded. This is called the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*. Thus was the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha* concluded. "Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma for the sake of restraint from taints pertaining only to this present life.
Nor, Cunda, do I teach the Dhamma solely for the sake of warding off taints pertaining only to future lives.
Rather, Cunda, I teach the Dhamma for the sake of restraint from taints pertaining to this present life as well as [those pertaining to future lives]."
And for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives.
Therefore, Cunda, that robe which has been permitted by me to you is sufficient only for warding off cold,
for warding off heat, for warding off the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and only for the purpose of covering the private parts.
That almsfood which has been permitted by me for you is sufficient,
just for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the cessation of affliction, and for support of the holy life;
thus I shall ward off old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be sustenance for me.
Blamelessness and a comfortable dwelling.
The lodging that has been permitted by me for you is sufficient merely for warding off cold,

for warding off heat, for warding off contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping creatures, and merely for the purpose of removing the perils of the climate and delighting in seclusion.

That medicinal requisites for the sick which have been permitted by me to you are sufficient only for the warding off of arisen painful feelings and for the sake of reaching the highest state of health.
9. Devotion to Pleasurable Things.
"It is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say:
'The ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, live devoted to the pursuit of pleasure.
Cunda, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be answered as follows:"
“What, friend, is this devotion to pleasure?
For there are many and various kinds of devotion to pleasure.
“Cunda, there are these four kinds of devotion to pleasure that are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial:”
They do not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment,
nor to Nibbāna. Which four?
In this case, Cunda, a certain fool, having repeatedly killed living beings, makes himself happy and satisfied.
This is the first devotion to pleasure.
Furthermore, Cunda, in this case, a certain person, having repeatedly taken what is not given, makes himself happy and satisfied.
This is the second devotion to pleasure.
Furthermore, Cunda, here someone, having repeatedly spoken falsehoods, makes himself happy and satisfied.
This is the third devotion to pleasure.
Furthermore, Cunda, here someone, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, indulges in them.
This is the fourth devotion to pleasure.
These, Cunda, are the four devotions to pleasure that are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial.
They do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment,
nor to Nibbāna. However, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this:
‘These ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, dwell devoted to these four kinds of devotion to pleasure.
You should say to them: ‘Do not speak thus.
If they were to speak thus, they would not be speaking rightly; they would be misrepresenting you with what is untrue and non-existent.
"Cunda, there are these four ways of devotion to pleasure that lead to complete disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
What are the four?

Here, Cunda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion."
This is the first devotion to pleasure.
Furthermore, Cunda, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna...
This is the second devotion to pleasure.
Furthermore, Cunda, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness.
This is the third pursuit of pleasure.

Furthermore, Cunda, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, a bhikkhu dwells in the fourth jhāna, which possesses neither-pain-nor-pleasure and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. This is the fourth pursuit of pleasure.
This is the fourth devotion to pleasure.
Cunda, these four devotions to pleasure lead to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
Now, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this:
‘These ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, dwell devoted to these four kinds of devotion to pleasure.
To them you should say, ‘So it is.
If they were to speak thus to you, they would be speaking rightly; they would not be misrepresenting you with what is untrue and non-existent.
10. The Benefits of Devoting Oneself to Pleasure Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this:
“But friends, for those who dwell devoted to these four ways of devoting oneself to pleasure, how many fruits and how many benefits are to be expected?”
Cunda, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
“Friends, for those who dwell devoted to these four modes of indulgence in pleasure, four fruits and four benefits are to be expected.
What are the four?”
"Here, friends, with the complete destruction of three fetters, a bhikkhu is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.
This is the first fruit, the first benefit.

Furthermore, friends, with the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, a bhikkhu is a once-returner; returning only once more to this world, he makes an end of suffering."
This is the second fruit, the second benefit.
Furthermore, friends, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, a bhikkhu is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This is the third fruit, the third benefit.

"Furthermore, friends, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
This is the fourth fruit, the fourth benefit.
These, friends, are the four fruits and four benefits to be expected for those who dwell devoted to the pursuit of these four kinds of pleasure."
11. The Impossibility for One Whose Taints Are Exhausted.
Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say:
"The ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, dwell as those whose nature is unstable."
Cunda, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:

"Friends, there are indeed teachings declared and prescribed by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, who is an Arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha—which are not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
Just as, friends, a city gatepost or an iron post, with its base deep and firmly planted, is immovable and unshakable;"

In the same way, friends, the Dhamma has been taught and laid down by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for his disciples, such that it is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.

Friends, a bhikkhu who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing nine points. Friends, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable... [of engaging in sexual misconduct]... [of taking what is not given]... [of speaking falsehood]... [of using intoxicants as a basis for negligence]... [of eating at the wrong time]... [of dancing, singing, music, or watching shows]...
[of adorning or beautifying himself with garlands, scents, or unguents]... [of accepting gold or silver]. Friends, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of these things.
A bhikkhu is incapable of taking what is not given, which is reckoned as theft; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse;

a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by means of hoarding, just as he did formerly when he was a householder; [a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is] incapable...
“A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of proceeding by way of favoritism; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of proceeding by way of aversion;
a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of proceeding by way of delusion; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of proceeding by way of fear.

That bhikkhu, friends, who is an arahant with taints destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—he is incapable of transgressing these nine points.”
12. Answering Questions.
“Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this:

‘Regarding the past, the ascetic Gotama proclaims an unlimited range of knowledge and vision, but regarding the future, he does not proclaim an unlimited range of knowledge and vision. What is the reason for this? How is this?’”
And those wanderers of other sects imagine that they should proclaim a knowledge and vision of one kind by means of a knowledge and vision of another kind, just like fools and the incompetent.
Cunda, regarding the past, the Tathāgata possesses a knowledge following memory;
he recollects as much as he wishes, for as long as he desires.
Furthermore, concerning the future, knowledge born of enlightenment arises in the Tathāgata:
“This is the final birth; now there is no further existence.
And if, Cunda, it concerns the past, and if it is untrue, incorrect, and not conducive to the goal, the Tathāgata does not declare it.
Cunda, even if something concerning the past is true, real, and beneficial, the Tathāgata does not explain it.
Cunda, even if something concerning the past is true, real, and beneficial, the Tathāgata knows the proper time for explaining that question.
Cunda, if something concerning the future is untrue, unreal, and unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not explain it... [and so on] ...for the explanation of that question.
“Cunda, if something concerning the present is unreal, untrue, and not conducive to the goal, the Tathāgata does not explain it.
Cunda, if something concerning the present is real and true but not conducive to the goal, the Tathāgata does not explain that either.
But if something concerning the present is real, true, and conducive to the goal, the Tathāgata knows the proper time to provide an explanation for that question.”

Thus, Cunda, regarding phenomena of the past, future, and present, the Tathāgata speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya; therefore he is called “the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Cunda, whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—[all that the Tathāgata knows as it really is].
With his mind, everything has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata;
therefore, he is called ‘the Tathāgata.
And, Cunda, between that night when the Tathāgata fully awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and that night [when he attains final nibbāna]...
He attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue; whatever he speaks, utters, or explains in the interval between these two events, all that is exactly so and not otherwise.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.”
“Cunda, the Tathāgata acts as he speaks, and speaks as he acts.
Because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is therefore called the ‘Tathāgata.

Cunda, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power; therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata.’”
13. The Point of the Undeclared.
Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say:
“Friends, does the Tathāgata exist after death? This alone is the truth, all else is foolishness.”
Cunda, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
"Friends, this has not been declared by the Blessed One:
'The Tathāgata exists after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.'"
"It is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say:
'But, friends, does the Tathāgata not exist after death? This alone is true, all else is false?
To those wanderers of other sects who speak thus, Cunda, you should say: "
"Friends, this too has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
'A Tathāgata does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolishness.
Now it is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say this:"
“But, friend, when wanderers of other sects say, ‘Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? This alone is the truth, all else is foolish,’ they should be told:
‘This, friends, has been left undeclared by the Blessed One. Thus, Cunda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed.
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false.
Now it is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say: ‘But, friends, why do you say:
“The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false”?’”
Cunda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be told this:
"Friends, even this has been left undeclared by the Blessed One:
'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.'"
"It is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say:
‘But why, friends, has this not been declared by the ascetic Gotama?
To wanderers of other sects who speak thus, Cunda, you should reply as follows:”
"Friend, this is not conducive to the goal, not conducive to the Dhamma, not fundamental to the holy life;
it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
Therefore, it was left undeclared by the Blessed One."
14. The Point of Exposition.
Furthermore, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say:
"But, friends, what has been declared by the ascetic Gotama?"
Cunda, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
"Friends, it has been declared by the Blessed One: 'This is suffering'; it has been declared by the Blessed One:
'This is the origin of suffering'; it has been declared by the Blessed One: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
“The practice, friend, has been declared by the Blessed One.
But it is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say this:
“But why, friends, has this been declared by the ascetic Gotama?”
Cunda, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
“For this, friends, is beneficial; this is connected with the Dhamma; this pertains to the fundamentals of the holy life;
it leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. Therefore, that...”
"It has been explained by the Blessed One.
"Cunda, those views based on the past which you hold, I have also explained them to you, exactly as they ought to be explained."
And since those [questions] are not to be explained, why should I explain them to you in that way?
Cunda, as for those views based on the future that have been declared by me, they too have been declared by me exactly as they are to be declared.
And since those are not to be declared, why should I declare them to you in that way?
"And what, Cunda, are those views concerning the past that you have declared to me—how they should be declared, and how they should not be declared?
Why should I declare them to you in that way?
There are, Cunda, some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view: [as follows]"
‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
Yet, Cunda, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘The self and the world are non-eternal... [and so on].
The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal … the self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal … the self and the world are self-made …
‘The self and the world are created by another… both created by oneself and by another… neither created by oneself nor by another,
but arisen fortuitously; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
‘Pleasure and pain are eternal… pleasure and pain are non-eternal… pleasure and pain are both eternal and non-eternal…’
Neither eternal nor non-eternal pleasure and pain...
pleasure and pain created by oneself...
pleasure and pain created by another...
‘Pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by another’ … ‘Pleasure and pain arise fortuitously,
being neither self-made nor made by another,’ and ‘This alone is true, all else is false.
In this regard, Cunda, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
Having approached them, I say this:
‘Is it the case, friends, that this is what you say?’”
“Is it that ‘the self and the world are eternal’?
And as for what they say to you:
“This alone is the truth, all else is false.”
I do not approve of that for them.
And why is that? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who perceive things differently.
“Cunda, even with this designation, I do not see anyone who is my equal, let alone my superior.
Rather, I am myself superior therein, namely, in regard to the supreme designation.
In this regard, Cunda, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:”
‘The self and the world are eternal… the self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal… the self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal…’
"The self and the world are created by oneself...
the self and the world are created by another...
the self and the world are created both by oneself and by another..."
The self and the world are neither created by oneself nor created by another, but have arisen fortuitously;
pleasure and pain are eternal … pleasure and pain are non-eternal … [and so forth].

‘Pleasure and pain are caused by another… pleasure and pain are caused both by oneself and by another… pleasure and pain arise fortuitously, being neither caused by oneself nor by another; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
Having approached them, I say this:
"Is it true, friends, that it is said:
'Pleasure and pain arise by chance, being neither made by oneself nor made by another'?"
And as for what they say to you:
"This alone is the truth, all else is false," I do not grant that to them.
And why is that? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who perceive things differently.
Even with this designation, Cunda, I do not see anyone equal to myself, much less superior.
But rather, it is I myself who am superior in this regard, namely, in higher designation (*adhipaññatti*).
Cunda, these are those views based on the past that I have explained to you, as they ought to be explained.
Since they are not to be explained [in other ways], why should I explain them to you otherwise?
16. Reliance on Views Concerning the Future.
And what, Cunda, are those reliance-views concerning the future that have been explained by me to you, as they ought to be explained;
and how they ought not to be explained—why should I explain them to you in that way?
"Cunda, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
'The self possesses form and is healthy after death; this alone is true, all else is false.
Yet, Cunda, there are some other ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:"
‘The self is formless… the self is both with form and formless… the self is neither with form nor formless…’
The self is percipient … the self is non-percipient … the self is neither percipient nor non-percipient …
"The self is annihilated and perishes; it does not exist after death. This alone is the truth, all else is vain.
In this regard, Cunda, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
"The self possesses form and is healthy after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain"—[they are wrong].
Having approached them, I say this:
"Is it the case, friends, that it is said:
'The self possesses form and is unimpaired after death'?"
And as for what they say to you:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false"—I do not grant them that.
And why is that? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who perceive things differently.
Even by this description, Cunda, I do not see anyone equal to myself, much less superior.
But I myself am superior in this regard, namely, in higher designation (*adhipaññatti*).
In this matter, Cunda, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as:
‘The self is formless…’”
The self is both material and immaterial;
the self is neither material nor immaterial;
the self is percipient...
‘The self is non-percipient… the self is neither percipient nor non-percipient… the self is annihilated,
perishes, and does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.’”
Having approached them, I say this:
"Is it true, friends, that it is said:
'The self is annihilated, perishes, and does not exist after death'?"
And as for what they say to you, Cunda:
"Only this is true, all else is false"—
that I do not concede to them.
And why is that? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who perceive things differently.
Even with this description, Cunda, I do not see anyone equal to myself, much less superior.
But I myself am superior in this regard, namely, through higher designation.
These, Cunda, are those dependencies on views associated with the future which I have explained to you, as they ought to be explained.
And since they are not to be explained [in other ways], why should I explain them to you otherwise?

And for the abandoning and transcending of these dependencies on views associated with the past and these dependencies on views associated with the future, Cunda, the four foundations of mindfulness have been taught and established by me.
What are the four?
Here, Cunda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating mind in mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

“Cunda, it is for the abandoning and the transcending of these dependencies on views associated with the past and these dependencies on views associated with the future that these four foundations of mindfulness have been taught and prescribed by me.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upavāṇa was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him.
Then the Venerable Upavāṇa said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
This Dhamma exposition is truly inspiring, Bhante;
it is most inspiring, Bhante. What is the name, Bhante, of this Dhamma exposition?”
“Therefore, Upavāṇa, you should remember this discourse on the Dhamma as ‘The Lovely.
This is what the Blessed One said.
The Venerable Upavāṇa was uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Pāsādika Sutta, the sixth, is finished.
